title: Try a New Idea With One Class, for One Week
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton addresses a professional-development problem rather than a classroom technique: teachers leave CPD, books and social media with more ideas than they can act on and struggle to know where to start. His answer, which he now uses to close his own CPD sessions, is a deliberately constrained commitment to try one idea, with one class, for one week. Each constraint is justified separately. One idea prevents overload and keeps the trial interpretable, since changing several things at once is a bad experiment whose results cannot be attributed. One class keeps the change manageable, and Barton advises choosing it strategically, whether for the strongest relationship or the biggest likely payoff, with primary teachers choosing a favourable time of week instead. One week keeps the stakes low, so a failed trial does little damage. The piece ends by building in a structured review: at week's end teachers evaluate, then tweak, ditch, extend or roll out the idea, and colleagues trying changes together meet to share what they learned.
points: Barton frames 'one idea' as an attribution rule as well as a workload rule: changing several inputs at once makes any change in outcome impossible to credit to a single cause.
The trial class should be chosen on purpose, either the class with the best relationship or the one where the idea promises the biggest impact; primary teachers pick a receptive time of week instead.
Limiting the trial to one week caps the downside, which makes it safe to try ideas that may well fail.
The week ends with a mandatory review that leads to a decision to tweak, ditch, extend with that class, or roll out to one more class.
When several colleagues trial changes together, the one-week cycle gives a natural point to meet and share what they tried and learned, turning individual experiments into departmental CPD.
quotes: Limiting yourself to just one idea is important to avoid being overwhelmed. It also allows you to better judge the effectiveness of that change - if you change more than one thing, it is like a bad science experiment where any change of outcome cannot be directly attributed as several inputs have changed.

Choosing just one class keeps the change manageable. I advise colleagues to choose their class carefully. It could be the one they have the best relationship with, or a class for which they feel the idea would have a big impact.
Finally, committing for just one week keeps the stakes small. If the change is a disaster - and it could well be - then not too much damage can be done in one week.
At the end of the week, colleagues must pause and evaluate. If things did not go to plan, why was that? Could a tweak make the difference?

If things did go well, can they try the idea even more with that class, or maybe roll it out with one additional class? If more than one person is trying to make a change, a week is a good time for colleagues to come together to share what they tried and what they learned.
